call: Order, please. The member for {riding} has the floor.

Order. I will hear the member for {riding}.

bill: Could the minister tell the House what {bill} will mean for communities like {riding}?
The people of {riding} have been waiting for {bill} for a long time. Can the minister tell the House when they'll see it working?
Would the minister explain to the House how {bill} delivers on what we promised in the election?
issue: Can the minister update the House on what the government is doing about {issue}?
People in {riding} ask me about {issue} every weekend. Could the minister tell them what's coming?
Would the minister tell the House how this government's plan on {issue} compares with the record of the party opposite?

bill: The minister has told this House twice that {bill} is ready. The people of {riding} have read it. When will the minister?
I want to support {bill}. So does my riding. Can the minister explain why the clause everyone back home asked about isn't in it?
Will the minister confirm that {bill} does for {riding} what the department's own briefing note says it won't?
issue: My constituents have heard the government's words on {issue}. What they haven't seen is a date. Does the minister have one?
The minister's department wrote to me about {issue} in the spring. It's autumn. Is the letter the plan?
I ask as a member of this caucus: on {issue}, is the minister speaking for the government or for the department?

offScript: I want to ask the minister about {issue}. Not the file. The thing itself. Has anyone in the department actually been to {riding} to look at it?
The minister won't find {issue} in the briefing book, because it's in {riding}. Will the minister come and see it with me?
Mr. Speaker, {issue}. The people who sent me here want to know whether this government has heard of it. Has the minister?

bill: Will the minister admit that {bill} does nothing for anyone who lives more than an hour from Ostrava?
Can the minister tell the House who was consulted on {bill}, and why none of them live in {riding}?
Why is the government rushing {bill} through this House when the people it affects haven't been asked?
issue: When will this government finally act on {issue}?
The minister has had years to deal with {issue}. Why are the people of {riding} still waiting?
Will the minister stand in this House and tell my constituents why {issue} isn't a priority for this government?

bill: On page nine of {bill} the minister's own officials wrote a number. It isn't the number the minister gave this House on Tuesday. Which one is true?
I have the minister's letter on {bill} from last spring, and I have the bill. They disagree. Which one should the people of {riding} believe?
The minister says {bill} was costed. Will the minister table the costing today, or tell the House why it can't be?
issue: The minister has said {issue} is being studied. I have the study. It was finished a year ago. What's the minister been doing since?
On {issue}, the minister's department has a plan it won't publish and a date it won't give. Which is the minister more embarrassed by?
Yesterday the minister said {issue} was a provincial matter. The minister's own website says otherwise. Would the minister like to correct one of them?

offScript: I'm going to ask the minister about {issue}, which is in {riding}, and which I'd wager the minister has never heard of. Have you?
Forget the talking points. {issue}. Does the minister know what it is, and what the government intends to do about it?
The minister's department has a file on {issue}. I know because I've read it, and it's two pages. Is that the government's answer to {riding}?

cooperative: I thank the member for {riding}, who has been tireless on this. The answer is yes, and soon, and I'd be happy to say more about it in the member's riding.
I'm glad the member asked. This government made a promise and this government is keeping it, and the member's constituents will see the difference.
guarded: I thank the member. The government's position is well known and well documented, and I refer the member to the department's statement of last month.
The member raises an important point. The government is seized of it. I have nothing to add to what has already been said.
angry: I thank the member, and I'd remind the party opposite, who are laughing, that they had years to deal with this and did nothing. Nothing.
The member's constituents deserve better than the heckling from across the aisle. This government is acting. The record speaks for itself.
anxious: I, ah, I thank the member for the question. The government takes this very seriously, and I will be making an announcement in due course.
The member is right to raise it. There is a process, the process is under way, and I'm advised that it's proceeding.

cooperative: I'd be happy to sit down with the member after Question Period and go through the file line by line. The short answer is: we're on it.
The member asks a fair question and deserves a full answer, which I'll give in writing. I don't want to mislead the House with a number from memory.
guarded: The member knows the matter is under review, and the member knows I can't say more than that from this chair.
I've answered that question before in this House. I'll refer the member to the record.
angry: The member should check with the member's own whip before asking a question like that in this House.
I'm not going to take lessons from the member on a file the member learned about from a newspaper.
anxious: The, ah, the matter is being looked at. I'll have more to say when the department has completed its work.
I'll take that under advisement and come back to the member.

cooperative: The member is right. The number was wrong. I'll correct the record this afternoon, and I'll apologise to the House for the confusion.
I don't have an answer to that today. I should. The member will have one by Friday.
guarded: I will take that under advisement.
I'm not in a position to answer that. I'll come back to the House.
angry: That is a cheap shot, and the member knows it, and I'm not going to dignify it with... I'll answer it in writing.
If the member had done the member's homework... No. No, I'll take the question. I'll take it. I don't have the figure in front of me.
anxious: I, ah. I'd have to check. I believe the figure the member has is, ah, it may be an earlier draft. I'll check.
That's, that's a question for... I'll have to get back to the member on that.

cooperative: I have heard of it, and I'd like to see it. If the member will have me, I'll come to {riding} before the House rises.
I'll look at {issue} myself. The member has my word, and the member knows what that's worth in this place.
guarded: {issue} is a matter the department is aware of. I'd caution the member against raising expectations in the member's riding that the government cannot meet.
I'm advised that {issue} falls largely to the province. The member may wish to take it up there.
angry: The member's riding is not the only riding in this country, and the member might remember that the next time the member stands up to grandstand.
The member wants a headline. Fine. Here it is: the government has a process, and {riding} will go through it like everyone else.
anxious: I, ah, I'm told the department has a file on it. I'll ask for it. I'll ask for it today.
I confess I don't know the particulars of {issue}. I'll find out. I'll write to the member.

lob: Your side thumps the desks on cue. Across the aisle, somebody says "softball" loud enough for Hansard.
A ripple of applause from your bench. The opposition doesn't look up from its phones.
The minister's parliamentary secretary gives you a thumbs-up. The gallery yawns.
parried: A few of your own side thump the desk, then stop when the whip turns around.
The opposition cheers a government member asking a real question. Your front bench does not.
Someone behind you mutters "brave." It doesn't sound like a compliment.
hit: A beat of silence on your own bench, then the opposition benches roar. The whip is looking at you.
The opposition thumps its desks for a government member. The minister's parliamentary secretary is writing something down.
The House goes very quiet, then very loud. Your own side stays quiet.
home: A couple of members from the rural caucus thump the desk. The minister's staff in the gallery flip through a binder.
Mild applause from behind you, louder from across the aisle. Somebody says the name of your riding like it's a punchline.
The whip's deputy makes a note. The member beside you says, "Well, that's on the record now."

lob: The scripted roar from your benches. The government side has heard it before and goes back to its correspondence.
Your side thumps on cue. The minister's answer gets the same from theirs.
The House leader nods once. You have done the job that was written for you.
parried: Your benches cheer the question and groan at the answer, in that order, as they always do.
A few of your side thump the desks. The minister's side laughs, which isn't the same as winning.
The critic beside you says, "Good try," and means it.
hit: Your whole side is on its feet, thumping the desks. The minister's front bench is looking at its shoes.
The roar from your benches drowns the Speaker. The minister sits down a beat too early.
Desks thumped, papers waved. The leader turns around to find out who you are.
home: Your benches cheer dutifully; it isn't the attack line they were promised. The government side looks up at the name of your riding.
A pause, then applause, from both sides of the House, which never happens.
The House leader frowns at the departure from the script. Two members from the rural caucus thump the desk anyway.

lob: The press gallery has moved on to the next question before the minister sits down.
A reporter in the gallery writes the word "planted" and underlines it.
Hansard records it. Nobody else does.
parried: A fair question, fairly deflected. The gallery notes the exchange and keeps it for a slow day.
One reporter looks up. The minister's answer gives them nothing to hang a story on.
A pointed question, and the minister took the point. The gallery writes down your name, at least.
hit: The press gallery, as one, reaches for its phones.
The minister's answer is already on three reporters' feeds before the Speaker calls the next question.
The clip is cut before the Speaker says "Order." It's your name on it.
home: The national press shrugs. The riding paper has already called your office for a comment.
A reporter from your end of the country asks a colleague how to spell the riding.
Nothing in the capital's papers. Everything in yours.
